1:
Who will not hold his peace is disputed at once. Gill reports that some make it God himself, silent while he does not arise for his people, and another Israel in captivity before settling on God or the church; his own judgment is that the prophet speaks, out of love for her. Clarke gives the words to God, declaring his purpose about what the last chapter had foretold. Ellicott lays the three options side by side, prophet, Servant or God, and prefers the second as most in harmony with what follows, the Servant carrying on what a later theology would call his mediatorial intercession. Wesley keeps the prophet and adds the interval, since the man resolving here lived near two hundred years before the thing was done. Henry keeps the prophet too and makes him a type of Christ, indefatigable in his office, instant in preaching and in prayer alike, since the business of ministers is to speak from God to his people and to God for his people, and in neither may they be silent.

Ellicott corrects the comparisons, reading the brightness of morning and a burning torch rather than the vaguer English.

Whether the new name is given or withheld divides them. Clarke supplies one outright and offers the name of the following verse as an alternative. Wesley finds it given there as well, one name answering to her condition and another to her relation. Keil and Delitzsch say new names take the place of the old. Ellicott alone reads the silence as deliberate, holding that the effect of the promise is heightened by the absence of the name, as something meant to transcend all experience.

The crown is examined more closely than the name. Ellicott distinguishes the two words, a kingly crown and a tiara like a high priest's mitre, notes that the two hands are different words with the second meaning the open palm, and concludes that the crown is not worn but held out: God is crowned from eternity already, and this new glory is displayed in the hand for the nations to gaze at. Gill keeps it in the hand for safety as much as for show, a crown of massy gold set with jewels that a prince looks at with pleasure and will not let be taken from him.

The two names are anchored in history by one voice only. Ellicott traces the first to Hezekiah's marriage with a queen of that name, which on the assumption of this prophet's authorship would have been fresh in his memory, and finds it after his manner to read an omen in a bride's name as in the names of his own sons; the confirmation, he adds, is that the word for Forsaken had itself been borne by an earlier queen. Clarke supplies the usage instead, that in the prophets a desolate land appears as a widow and an inhabited land as a married woman with husband and children.

The last verse is felt as a difficulty. Gill refuses any allusion to sons marrying their mother as exceedingly disagreeable, prefers the older versions that read dwell with rather than marry, and would render it that thy sons shall have thee. Clarke attacks the text, since the particles of comparison are missing from the Hebrew though the versions seem to have read them, probably lost by a copyist; he reports a scholar who would read builder instead of sons and remarks that little is gained by it, and cites a traveller for the eastern custom by which the unmarried take virgins and widowers widows. Ellicott turns the figure round instead, making the people in their collective unity the bridegroom and the country the bride, whom they are bound as a husband to cherish and protect. Keil and Delitzsch let the words stand.
6:
Who the watchmen are is settled by elimination. Gill runs through the rejected identifications, angels, kings, magistrates and the mourners in Zion, and settles on ministers of the gospel, drawing out the figure of men set on a city wall who must keep their stand, descry an enemy and defend the outworks, which asks courage, constancy, vigilance and sobriety. Ellicott reduces the field to two, angelic guardians or prophets, allows that two passages may be pleaded for the first, and prefers the second, instancing the prophets of the return and of the Christian church. Henry takes the same view and presses the duty: the church is a besieged city, so its sentinels must be wakeful and willing to endure hardness, never off watch while those they watch for are in danger, and never betraying the cause by a cowardly silence.

Clarke alone reconstructs the practice behind it. He takes it from the temple service, where a constant watch was kept day and night by the Levites, this part seemingly falling to the singers; the eastern watches, he says, are still kept by a loud cry raised from time to time, to mark the hour and prove the watchman awake, which is why they are elsewhere told to lift up the voice and why the bitterest reproach against them is that they are dumb dogs. He reads a short psalm as nothing but the alternating cry of two divisions of that watch, the first calling on the second to bless the Lord and the second answering with a set blessing.

The people addressed beside them get their proper title. Ellicott corrects the English to the remembrancers, whose office is to remind God of his promises day and night until Jerusalem is a praise in the earth. Wesley keeps both senses, men who put God in mind of his promise and men who make the Lord remembered by putting his people in mind of him. Henry adds that people must not think it enough that their watchmen pray for them.

The oath raises the question what God swears by. Gill reports the view that the arm is Christ and rejects it on precise ground, that God is said to swear to him and about him but never by him, so omnipotence is meant; the force of it is that God stakes his being the omnipotent God he is on the performance. Ellicott recognises the principle of a later epistle, that God can swear by nothing less than what is identified with his own greatness, and sets the promise against the curse of the law it reverses. Keil and Delitzsch state the result, that the church will no longer succumb to worldly power. On the eating in the courts Clarke finds the law behind the phrase, the tithe being eaten before the Lord and the fruit of a fourth year holy for praise; Ellicott renders it of my sanctuary and has the harvest and vintage feasts kept as of old.

Whose gates are to be gone through divides them. Gill takes them for the gates of the church in the latter day, open night and day so converts of either nation may enter. Henry keeps the historical picture, the gates of Babylon thrown open, causeways cast up, stones gathered out, standards set up so the returning people may embody for safety. Ellicott hears the prophet crying to heralds who summon the exiles, and argues from the plural, peoples rather than people, that the Gentiles are thought of as escorting Israel, which makes the command addressed to the returning exiles. Clarke closes on the four names and finds them in inverted order, since God's not forsaking comes first, then his seeking, then the redemption, and holiness last as the consequence of all three; Ellicott hears in the last a deliberate answer to the name of forsaking given earlier.
